Forecasts: in Türkiye, hourly and daily temperatures and the weather come from the Turkish State Meteorological Service (MGM); elsewhere, and for rain, UV and pressure everywhere, from Open-Meteo.com (CC BY 4.0). In France the Météo-France models (AROME and ARPEGE) and in the United Kingdom and Ireland the Met Office models are used through Open-Meteo. The ECMWF model (IFS and AIFS, © ECMWF, CC BY 4.0) is used through Open-Meteo as a backup and for comparison. Current conditions are checked against the nearest station: MGM stations in Türkiye, airport reports (METAR) from the NOAA Aviation Weather Center elsewhere. Air quality: Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) through Open-Meteo (CC BY 4.0). Place search: Photon, © OpenStreetMap contributors.

The feels-like temperature is how warm or cold the air feels on your skin. Wind carries heat away from the body and makes it feel colder; humidity makes it harder to cool down and makes it feel warmer. It is worked out from the temperature, the humidity and the wind. Dress for this number rather than for the actual temperature.

Wind speed is the average speed of the air ten metres above the ground. A gust is a sudden burst that lasts a few seconds and can be much stronger than the average. The arrows show where the wind is blowing to. Above 40 km/h umbrellas struggle and cycling gets hard; above 60 km/h loose things outside should be secured.

Relative humidity tells how much water vapour the air holds compared with the most it could hold at that temperature. Between 40% and 60% feels comfortable for most people. The dew point is the temperature at which that vapour turns into dew: above about 18° the air feels sticky, below 10° it feels dry. High humidity makes heat harder to bear and laundry slower to dry.

The UV index measures the strength of the sun\'s ultraviolet rays that burn the skin. It is highest around midday and on clear summer days, and clouds lower it only partly. From 3 upwards sunscreen is a good idea; from 6 upwards add a hat, sunglasses and shade at midday. From 8 upwards the skin can burn in under half an hour.

Visibility is the distance at which a large object can still be seen clearly. Fog, mist, heavy rain, snow and dust all reduce it. Below 1 km there is fog and driving needs great care; between 1 and 5 km the air is misty or hazy. Clear air often means views of 20 km and more.

Air pressure is the weight of the air above you, reduced to sea level so that places can be compared. About 1013 hPa is normal. Falling pressure usually means the weather may turn: cloud, wind and rain are on the way. Rising pressure usually brings calmer, clearer weather. The direction of the change matters more than the number itself.

Cloud cover is the share of the sky that is covered by cloud. Under 20% the sky is clear; above 85% it is overcast. Thin, high clouds can cover the whole sky and still let the sun through, while low, thick clouds block it. Clear nights cool down faster; cloudy nights stay milder.

The chance of precipitation is how likely it is that at least a little rain or snow falls at your place in that hour. The amount, in millimetres, tells how much: 1 mm is one litre of water on each square metre. Under 1 mm an hour is light, 1 to 4 mm is steady rain, more is heavy. A high chance with a small amount means a brief, light shower.

Sunrise and sunset are the moments when the upper edge of the sun crosses the horizon. The time between them is the length of the day; it grows from late December to late June and shrinks for the rest of the year. It stays light for about half an hour before sunrise and after sunset. The UV is strongest when the sun is highest, around the middle of the day.

The European Air Quality Index sums up how clean the air is, from the pollutant that is worst at that moment: fine particles, ozone, nitrogen dioxide or sulphur dioxide. Fine particles (PM2.5) matter most for health because they reach deep into the lungs. The values are a model forecast from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service for an area of about ten kilometres, so a busy street can be worse than the number shown. Air is often worst on calm, cold mornings and during rush hours.

The moon does not shine by itself; we see the half that the sun lights up. As it circles the Earth in about 29 and a half days, we see more and then less of that lit half: from the new moon, which is invisible, through the first quarter to the full moon and back. The moon rises about 50 minutes later each day. Around the full moon it is up all night and its light hides faint stars; around the new moon the sky is at its darkest. Everything on this page is calculated on your phone.
